title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Tidy Data: The Assumed Shape

Tidy data follows three rules: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell. Every tidyverse tool assumes this shape.
When your data doesn’t conform, you fix the data — not the tools.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The Grammar of Data Manipulation






dplyr provides a consistent set of verbs for data manipulation:



Verb
Does




select()
Picks variables based on their names.


filter()
Picks cases based on their values.


mutate()
Add or transform columns


summarize()
Reduces multiple values down to a single summary.


arrange()
Reorder rows


group_by()
Apply operations by group



These all combine naturally. Learning the verbs is learning the language.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
A Note on Subsetting
Before we use these verbs, let’s ground ourselves in base R subsetting — it’s what dplyr builds on. Understanding the foundation makes the syntax sugar more transparent.
You already know base R subsetting. Here’s the vocabulary:

df <- data.frame(country = c("USA", "Brazil", "India"),
                 pop     = c(3e6, 2e6, 1.4e9))

df[1, 2]          # row 1, col 2 — matrix style
#> [1] 3e+06
df[["pop"]]       # column by name — list style
#> [1] 3.0e+06 2.0e+06 1.4e+09
df$pop            # column shorthand
#> [1] 3.0e+06 2.0e+06 1.4e+09








Important


Never subset by row number in a script:

gapminder[19:70, ]   # ❌ not self-documenting, breaks if data changes

Always subset by condition — it is explicit, readable, and robust.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
filter() — Keep Rows by Condition

filter() takes logical (binary) expressions and returns the rows in which all conditions are TRUE.
filter() does NOT impact columns
the data.frame is ALWAYS the fist argument
Lets find all rows in gapminder that in which the life expectancy is less then 40



filter(gapminder, lifeExp < 40)
#> # A tibble: 124 × 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
#> # ℹ 121 more rows

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
filter() — Multiple Conditions
Comma-separated conditions are treated as AND:

filter(gapminder, lifeExp < 40, year == 2007)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   country   continent  year lifeExp     pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>     <fct>     <int>   <dbl>   <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Swaziland Africa     2007    39.6 1133066     4513.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
filter() — The %in% Operator

filter(gapminder,
       country %in% c("Iraq", "Iran", "Afghanistan"),
       year > 2005)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       2007    43.8 31889923      975.
#> 2 Iran        Asia       2007    71.0 69453570    11606.
#> 3 Iraq        Asia       2007    59.5 27499638     4471.








Tip


%in% tests membership in a vector — much cleaner than chaining | (OR) conditions. You’ll use it constantly with site numbers, HUC codes, and state names in water resources work. %in% maps directly to SQL IN.

text:
select() — Keep Columns by Name
select() can be used to remove columns. The ! negates a selection


Select columns:

select(gapminder, country, lifeExp)
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 2
#>   country     lifeExp
#>   <fct>         <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan    28.8
#> 2 Afghanistan    30.3
#> 3 Afghanistan    32.0
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows


Rename while selecting:

select(gapminder, country, life_exp = lifeExp)
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 2
#>   country     life_exp
#>   <fct>          <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan     28.8
#> 2 Afghanistan     30.3
#> 3 Afghanistan     32.0
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The |> Pipe Operator
The pipe passes the object on the left into the first argument of the function on the right:


Without pipe:

select(gapminder, country, lifeExp)
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 2
#>   country     lifeExp
#>   <fct>         <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan    28.8
#> 2 Afghanistan    30.3
#> 3 Afghanistan    32.0
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows


With pipe:

gapminder |>
  select(country, lifeExp)
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 2
#>   country     lifeExp
#>   <fct>         <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan    28.8
#> 2 Afghanistan    30.3
#> 3 Afghanistan    32.0
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows



Keyboard shortcut: Cmd+Shift+M (Mac) / Ctrl+Shift+M (Windows)
The pipe is what makes dplyr readable — it lets you build a chain of operations that reads like a sentence:

text:
mutate() — Add New Columns

mutate() defines and inserts new variables into a existing data.frame
mutate() builds new variables sequentially so you can reference earlier ones when defining later ones
In the gapminder dataset we have a population and gdp per capita variable. Lets calculate the GDP of each county

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
summarize() — Collapse to a Summary
summarize() takes n rows and returns 1:

gapminder |>
  mutate(gdp = pop * gdpPercap) |>
  summarize(mean_gdp = mean(gdp),
            sd_gdp   = sd(gdp))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>        mean_gdp        sd_gdp
#>           <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 186809560507. 714029666918.


Useful summary functions: mean(), median(), sd(), min(), max(), sum(), n(), n_distinct(), quantile()

orders the rows of a data.frame rows by the values of selected columns.

group_by() + summarize() — Split-Apply-Combine
Have you ever needed:

Mean wind speed by storm type?
Average discharge by HUC?
Case counts by state?


group_by() adds grouping structure. mutate() and summarize() honor it:

gapminder |>
  mutate(gdp = pop * gdpPercap) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(mean_gdp = mean(gdp),
            sd_gdp   = sd(gdp))
#> # A tibble: 12 × 3
#>    year     mean_gdp        sd_gdp
#>   <int>        <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1  1952 49561190904. 197218416124.
#> 2  1957 62649777593. 233501965317.
#> 3  1962 77495568413. 279956456279.
#> # ℹ 9 more rows

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Why Visualization?
Data without visualization is just numbers. Before building any model or writing any interpretation, plot your data. Always.

ggplot2 is built on a consistent grammar — the same recipe works for scatter plots, line charts, heatmaps, and beyond. This systematic grammar is what makes ggplot2 powerful: once you learn the components, you can build any visualization.
The Grammar of Graphics says every chart is built from the same small set of components:

Data — what are we visualizing?
Aesthetic mappings — which variables map to which visual properties?
Geometries — what shape represents the data?
Labels, facets, themes — everything else

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The ggplot2 Workflow
Building a plot is additive — you layer components with +:

DATA |>
  ggplot(aes(x = VAR1, y = VAR2)) +
  GEOM_FUNCTION() +
  ... +
  LABELS +
  FACETS +
  THEME








Tip


Notice the switch from |> (pipe) to + (plus) when you enter ggplot. The pipe passes data into ggplot(); the plus adds layers within the plot. This is the most common source of syntax errors when learning ggplot.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 1: The Canvas

gm2007 <- filter(gapminder, year == 2007)

ggplot(data = gm2007)

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 1: Add Aesthetic Mappings

ggplot(data = gm2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))


Aesthetic mappings describe how variables in the data are visualized. Placed in ggplot(), they apply globally to all layers.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 2: Add a Geometry

ggplot(data = gm2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point()

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Fixed vs. Data-Driven Aesthetics


Fixed — set outside aes(), applies to all points:

ggplot(data = gm2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(col = "red")









Data-driven — set inside aes(), varies by data:

ggplot(data = gm2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(col = continent))

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Multiple Geoms



ggplot(data = gm2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 3: Labels



ggplot(data = gm2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 4: Facets



ggplot(data = gm2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp))

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
facet_wrap() vs. facet_grid()


facet_wrap(~x): one faceting variable, auto-wraps into rows/columns — flexible layout
facet_grid(y~x): two faceting variables, strict row-column grid — enforces structure

Use facet_wrap() for many categories without hierarchy; facet_grid() for structured two-way comparisons.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Step 5: Themes
Themes control all non-data visual elements:

ggplot(data = gm2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop)) +
  labs(x = "Per Capita GDP", y = "Life Expectancy",
       title = "GDP vs. Life Expectancy (2007)") +
  theme_minimal()



Built-in themes: theme_bw(), theme_minimal(), theme_light(), theme_dark(), theme_classic()
The ggthemes package adds Economist, WSJ, FiveThirtyEight, and many more.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Saving Plots
ggplot outputs are objects — assign them, then save:

p <- ggplot(data = gm2007, aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = continent, size = pop)) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave(p,
       file   = "img/gdp-lifeexp-2007.png",
       width  = 8,
       height = 5,
       units  = "in")








Tip


Always save with explicit width, height, and units. The default dimensions rarely match what you need for reports or publications. fig.retina = 3 in your chunk options gives you high-DPI output for web rendering.

section: When One Table Is Not Enough
text:
When One Table Is Not Enough
Real data rarely lives in a single tidy table. You will always need to combine information from multiple sources:

Flow records from one table + watershed area from another
Species counts from field surveys + climate data from NOAA
County-level discharge + census population estimates


Multiple related tables are called relational data. The relations are as important as the data itself.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The Anatomy of a Join
Before writing a _join() call, answer three questions:

What is the key? Which column(s) connect the two tables?
What is the relationship? One-to-one, or one-to-many?
What happens to non-matching rows? Keep them or drop them?

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Keys
A key is the variable (or set of variables) that uniquely identifies an observation:

Primary key: uniquely identifies rows in its own table
Foreign key: uniquely identifies rows in another table





band_members

#>   name  band   
#>   <chr> <chr>  
#> 1 Mick  Stones 
#> 2 John  Beatles
#> 3 Paul  Beatles




band_instruments
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   name  plays 
#>   <chr> <chr> 
#> 1 John  guitar
#> 2 Paul  bass  
#> 3 Keith guitar


name is the primary key in both tables and the foreign key that connects them.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The Silent Failure Modes






Important


Bad joins fail silently — your code runs, your result looks plausible, but the numbers are wrong.
Failure 1: Wrong join type
Using inner_join when you meant left_join silently drops rows. Your dataset shrinks and you may not notice until a downstream result is unexpectedly small.
Failure 2: Non-unique key
If the key column is not actually unique in one of the tables, every matching row gets duplicated. Your dataset grows and you may not notice.




Always verify after joining:

# 1. Row count unchanged
nrow(result) == nrow(left_table)

# 2. No unexpected NAs in joined columns
sum(is.na(result$new_column))

# 3. Spot-check a known value
result |> filter(key == "known_value") |> distinct(key, new_column)

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Surrogate Keys
Sometimes a table has no natural primary key. Create one with row_number():

gapminder |>
  slice(1:5) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap    id
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.     1
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.     2
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.     3
#> # ℹ 2 more rows

This is called a surrogate key — it has no real-world meaning but uniquely identifies each row for joining purposes.

section: Real Example: NWIS Flow + Site Metadata
text:
Real Example: NWIS Flow + Site Metadata

# Two tables, one key
flow      # site_no appears thousands of times (foreign key)
site_meta # site_no appears once per gauge (primary key)

# One-to-many join: one site_meta row fans out to thousands of flow rows
flow_meta <- flow |>
  left_join(site_meta, by = "site_no")

# Verify
nrow(flow_meta) == nrow(flow)                    # row count unchanged?
sum(is.na(flow_meta$drain_area_va)) == 0          # no missing area values?
flow_meta |>                                      # known value check
  filter(site_no == "09380000") |>
  distinct(site_no, drain_area_va)               # should be ~111,800 mi²

This is exactly the join you will perform in Lab 1.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The Same Data, Many Shapes
The same underlying data can be stored in multiple ways. Which is easiest to work with depends on what you want to do:






Wide format — one row per country:

#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   country  year lifeExp gdpPercap
#>   <fct>   <int>   <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Brazil   1952    50.9     2109.
#> 2 Brazil   2007    72.4     9066.
#> 3 India    1952    37.4      547.
#> # ℹ 1 more row


Long format — one row per country-year-metric:

#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   country  year metric     value
#>   <fct>   <int> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 Brazil   1952 lifeExp     50.9
#> 2 Brazil   1952 gdpPercap 2109. 
#> 3 Brazil   2007 lifeExp     72.4
#> # ℹ 5 more rows

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
Tidy Data: The Standard

Three rules that tidyverse tools assume:

Each variable has its own column
Each observation has its own row
Each value has its own cell


In practice: put each dataset in a tibble, put each variable in a column. The rest follows.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
The World Is Messy

Real data almost never arrives tidy. Two common problems:

A variable is spread across multiple columns — column names are values, not variable names
An observation is scattered across multiple rows — a single record spans several rows

tidyr (part of tidyverse) fixes both.

    cols      = -country,         # pivot everything except country
    names_to  = "year",
    values_to = "lifeExp"
  )
#> # A tibble: 24 × 3
#>   country year  lifeExp
#>   <fct>   <chr>   <dbl>
#> 1 Brazil  1952     50.9
#> 2 Brazil  1957     53.3
#> 3 Brazil  1962     55.7

pivot_wider() — Long to Wide
When one observation is scattered across multiple rows, pivot wider:


table_long |>

              values_from = value)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   country  year lifeExp gdpPercap

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
When to Use Each Format


Long format is better for:

ggplot2 — it expects one row per observation
group_by() + summarize() — aggregating over a variable
Time series with multiple variables
Repeated measures data


Wide format is better for:

Linear models where each variable is a predictor
Sharing data with non-technical audiences
Correlation matrices
When few variables and many observations

What Is Quantitative Reasoning?







Working Definition: Thinking about data from our world to better understand and make choices about the past, present, and future.


Many people can work with data (data scientists)
Many people have domain knowledge (hydrologists)
Few can do both carefully — that’s what makes you valuable

The rest of today is about building the foundation for that focusing on how computers store, find, and interpret information — and why that matters for doing science well.

title: Week 1
section: Every Analysis Is a File Problem
text:
Every Analysis Is a File Problem
Every piece of work in this course — and in your career — follows this chain:

Raw Data          ← files on disk, often from URLs or APIs
  ↓ R Scripts     ← read, clean, transform
Processed Data    ← files on disk
  ↓ R Scripts     ← model, summarize, visualize  
Outputs           ← figures, tables, reports — files on disk


A broken link anywhere in this chain means the analysis cannot be reproduced.
A file you can’t find, a path that only works on your machine, a format no one else can open — these are not minor inconveniences. They are scientific failures.



“An analysis is only as reproducible as the data you can find next year.”

title: Week 1
text:
The Computer






Three subsystems you need to understand:

Disk: Persistent storage — files live here when the power is off. Reading from disk is slow.
Memory (RAM): Ephemeral workspace — data lives here while R runs. Fast, but finite and temporary.
CPU: Executes instructions — does the computation.

Why this matters for you:
When you load a 4 GB raster into R, it moves from disk into RAM. If your RAM is full, R crashes or slows to a crawl. Knowing where the bottleneck is (I/O? memory? compute?) is how you diagnose and fix slow analyses.

title: Week 1
text:
The Compute Cycle


Data flows: disk → memory → CPU → memory → disk
Every read_csv(), st_read(), and rast() call you make starts this cycle. Every write_csv() and writeRaster() ends it.

title: Week 1
text:
Bits and Bytes







A bit is one logical state: 0 or 1
A byte is 8 bits
Everything on a computer — text, images, spatial data, model outputs — is bytes

Why it matters in practice:



Dataset
Size estimate




USGS daily flow record, 1 gauge, 50 years
~150 KB


NHDPlus HR flowlines, CONUS
~12 GB


NWM retrospective, 1 variable, 1 year
~200 GB


3DEP 1m DEM, single HUC4
~8–40 GB















These numbers stop being surprising once you know the unit chain: KB → MB → GB → TB (each ×1,024).

title: Week 1
text:
What Is a File?







Files save bytes on disk in a structured, meaningful way
Every file has three key properties:

A name — how you and the computer identify it
A path — its address in the file system hierarchy
An extension — tells programs how to interpret the bytes

Hard drives don’t understand files — they store bytes. The file system is the organizational layer that makes bytes into named, navigable objects.

title: Week 1
text:
File Systems & Directories






How operating systems differ:

Windows  : drives (C:\), backslash separators
macOS / Linux  : forward slashes, everything under root /
Cloud (S3, GCS): looks like a filesystem, but is actually flat key-value storage

Key vocabulary:



Term
Meaning




Root
Top-level directory — contains everything


Working directory
Where your session is (getwd())


Parent directory
One level up (..)


Subdirectory
A folder inside the working directory

title: Week 1
text:
The Importance of Names






Tip


“There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.” ~Phil Karlton



File names are how you — and your collaborators — navigate a project. There is no enforced standard. The decisions are always yours.
Bad names compound silently. One bad name is annoying. A project full of them is a crisis.

Three Principles

Machine readable — unambiguous, parseable, regex-friendly
Human readable — tells you what’s inside without opening it
Sortable — natural order reflects logical order

title: Week 1
text:
Machine Readable

No spaces, no punctuation, no accented characters, no mixed case
Use regular expression friendly (e.g. use patterns!)
Use ISO 8601 dates: YYYY-MM-DD — they sort correctly as strings
Consistent delimiters:

_ separates metadata fields
- separates words within a field



This makes files easy to …

text:
Human Readable + Sortable
Human readable — the name communicates content and purpose. Here, we see the order that the files run (utilities, download, clean, analyze, figures), the project they belong to (src), are archived in the file names.

list.files("R")
#> [1] "00_src_utils.R"         "01_src_data-download.R" "02_src_data-clean.R"   
#> [4] "03_src_analysis.R"      "04_src_figures.R"


#>   Order Project       Purpose extension

#> 2    01     src data-download         R
#> 3    02     src    data-clean         R
#> 4    03     src      analysis         R
#> 5    04     src       figures         R

title: Week 1
text:
Absolute vs. Relative Paths
Absolute — starts from root, always resolves, but only on your machine:

img <- png::readPNG('/Users/mikejohnson/github/csu-523c-2026/slides/img/03-bit-byte.png')


Relative — starts from the working directory, works anywhere the project is opened:

img <- png::readPNG('img/03-bit-byte.png')



. and .. shorthand:
.    = this directory
..   = the parent directory

../data/raw/flow.csv   →  up one level, then into data/raw/








Important


Absolute paths are the #1 reproducibility killer in shared projects. If your code contains /Users/yourname/, it will break the moment anyone else runs it — including future you on a new machine.

title: Week 1
text:
RStudio Projects + here






Tip


RStudio Projects (.Rproj) automatically set the working directory to the project root when opened — making relative paths reliable by default.



Best practices:

Keep all project files together: raw data, scripts, outputs, figures
Never hardcode paths outside the project root
Use here::here() for paths inside packages or Quarto documents — it anchors to the project root regardless of where the .qmd lives


# Always resolves from project root, never from the .qmd file's location
here::here("data", "raw", "flow_2024.csv")
#> /Users/mikejohnson/github/csu-523c-2026/data/raw/flow_2024.csv

title: Week 1
text:
What Extensions Tell Us
# Wrong reader:
img <- jpeg::readJPEG('img/03-bit-byte.png')
#> Error: file is not in JPEG format
# Correct reader:
img <- png::readPNG('img/03-bit-byte.png')
dim(img)    #> 394 768 3  (rows × cols × channels)
class(img)  #> "array"



Extensions are metadata that tell programs how to interpret bytes. The file itself doesn’t change — only the interpretation does.
The bytes on disk are identical in both calls. The reader determines what you get back.

title: Week 1
text:
URLs Are Just Remote Paths
The file system logic you just learned applies directly to URLs:
https://mikejohnson51.github.io/csu-ess-330/slides/1-welcome.html#/title-slide
         ↑ server (domain)      ↑ directory   ↑ file             ↑ anchor

s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds/CONUS/zarr/chrtout.zarr
     ↑ bucket                        ↑ directory  ↑ file

And URLs are your data pipeline:

# USGS streamflow — the path IS the query
url <- "https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv/?sites=06752260&parameterCd=00060&format=json"
data <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)

dplyr::glimpse(data)(data)

# NWM retrospective on S3 — same concept, different protocol
s3_path <- "s3://noaa-nwm-retrospective-3-0-pds/CONUS/zarr/chrtout.zarr"



Query parameters (?sites=...&parameterCd=...) filter data at the server before it reaches your machine. Understanding URL structure means understanding how to ask for exactly what you need.

About This Course
This course focuses on analyzing and understanding water resources through the lens of modern data science. Building on the foundational R skills from ESS/WR 523a, we examine key innovations in data science, geospatial processing and machine learning for hydrological prediction and model parameterization — with an emphasis using real data.
Every dataset, every example, and every lab draws from systems you will encounter in professional practice. The course is organized around a single professional question: what does it take to turn raw environmental data into a reproducible, publishable result that informs real decisions? Each week answers a piece of that question with a different class of data and methods — from spatial analysis through to machine learning workflows applied directly to hydrological problems.
By the end of the course you will have built a public portfolio of six published analyses spanning data wrangling, vector data, raster data, machine learning, and time series — using the same data infrastructure that federal agencies and consulting firms use operationally.

All files store bits.
Extensions can be considered a type of metadata that provides information about the way data might be stored
There are 1000’s of different formats for data ranging from common to custom

text:
Publish via GitHub Pages (recommended: simple main → docs workflow)
Preferred workflow (concise): students create their own GitHub repository, configure Quarto to render into a docs/ folder, push main, enable Pages, and submit the Pages URL. This keeps the course repo untouched and makes grading easy.
Quick steps:

Create a personal repo on GitHub (e.g., csu-523c) and clone it into ~/github/.
In the repo root add a _quarto.yml with website: output-dir: docs (example below). This makes quarto render write into docs/ automatically.

quarto.yml (minimal):
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "csu-523c"
  output-dir: docs

title: Lab 1: Data Science Tools
text:
In January 2023, the federal government announced the first-ever Tier 3 shortage on the Colorado River — triggering mandatory cuts to Arizona, Nevada, and Mexico. Those cuts were calculated from streamflow records like the ones you are about to pull.
The Colorado River Basin supplies drinking water to 40 million people across 7 US states, irrigates 5 million acres of farmland, and is governed by one of the oldest and most contested water rights agreements in American history — the Colorado River Compact of 1922. Understanding how streamflow varies across this system is not an academic exercise. It is the daily work of water managers, federal agencies, tribal water rights holders, and scientists navigating a river under compounding stress from drought, overallocation, and climate change.
In this lab you will work with real streamflow records pulled directly from the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) — the same federal system water managers query every morning. You will build a complete analytical pipeline: from raw API call to normalized comparisons, threshold detection, basin-wide trend visualization, and a predictive model of the Compact’s key accounting point.

Data
We will use the dataRetrieval package — developed and maintained by the USGS — to pull 44 years of daily mean discharge from 7 long-record gauges spanning the Colorado River’s main stem and major tributaries.
The USGS parameter code for discharge is 00060 (cubic feet per second). The statistic code 00003 is the daily mean value. Under the hood, dataRetrieval constructs and queries the same REST API URL we explored in lecture:
https://waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/dv/?sites=09380000&parameterCd=00060&statCd=00003
The data can be grabbed below!

title: Lab 1: Data Science Tools
text:
The anatomy of a join
Before writing a single _join() call, answer three questions:

What is the key? Which column(s) connect the two tables?
What is the relationship? One-to-one, or one-to-many?
What happens to non-matching rows? Keep them (with NAs), or drop them?







The (main) four joins — and when to use each











Function
Keeps rows from…
Non-matching rows




left_join(x, y)
All of x
y columns filled with NA


right_join(x, y)
All of y
x columns filled with NA


inner_join(x, y)
Only rows matching in both
Dropped entirely


full_join(x, y)
Both x and y
NAs on whichever side has no match



The most common mistake: using inner_join when you meant left_join. An inner join silently drops every row from x that has no match in y — your dataset shrinks and you may not notice until downstream results are wrong.
The second most common mistake: joining on a key that is not unique in one of the tables. If site_no appears twice in site_meta, every matching row in your flow data will be duplicated — your dataset grows and you may not notice.
Both failures are invisible without explicit verification. For graduate-level work, in your write-up briefly justify the join type you chose, quantify any unmatched keys or duplicates you observed, and discuss possible data provenance reasons for mismatches.


a. Pull site metadata for all 7 gauges. Before joining, verify that site_no is actually unique in site_meta — a duplicated key will silently inflate your row count.


Code
site_meta <- readNWISsite(gauges$site_no) |>
  select(
    site_no,
    drain_area_va,   # drainage area in square miles
    huc_cd,          # 8-digit HUC watershed code
    dec_lat_va,      # latitude
    dec_long_va      # longitude
  )

# Is site_no actually unique? If any row shows n > 1, the join will duplicate rows
site_meta |> count(site_no) |> filter(n > 1)


[1] site_no n      
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)








Keys: primary and foreign



A primary key uniquely identifies each row in its own table. site_no in site_meta is a primary key — exactly one row per gauge.
A foreign key appears in another table to link observations back. site_no in your flow data is a foreign key — it appears thousands of times (once per day per gauge) and connects each observation to its gauge’s metadata.
The join matches on this shared key. Because one gauge has many flow records, this is a one-to-many relationship — one site_meta row fans out to match thousands of flow rows.


b. Join site_meta to your flow data using site_no as the key. Use the join type that keeps all flow records regardless of whether metadata is available.
c. Verify the join — this step is not optional:






Always verify your joins — three checks, every time




nrow(result) == nrow(left_table) — row count unchanged ✓
sum(is.na(new_column)) == 0 — no unexpected NAs ✓
Spot-check a known value — numbers are plausible ✓

These checks cost 30 seconds and catch errors that would otherwise corrupt every downstream calculation silently. You will join data in every lab this semester. Consider, building this habit now.

Model Building
b. Fit a linear model predicting log_lees from log_glenwood, season, and their interaction, If you haven’t seen linear modeling in R, we will cover it in more detail latter in this course, but, the syntax is straightforward: lm(response ~ predictor1 * predictor2, data = mydata) fits a model with main effects and an interaction term. The interaction (*) allows the relationship between Glenwood and Lees to differ by season while a model without interaction (lm(log_lees ~ log_glenwood + season)) would assume the same Glenwood-Lees relationship in every season.


Code
mod <- lm(log_lees ~ log_glenwood * season, data = lees_model_data)
summary(mod)


c. In 3–4 sentences: (1) report the R² and state whether the overall model is statistically significant, (2) interpret the log_glenwood coefficient as an elasticity — what does it mean physically that the coefficient is greater than 1? (3) describe what the significant negative interaction terms tell you about the upstream-downstream relationship outside of Snowmelt season.






Tip



In a log-log model, the coefficient on log_glenwood is an elasticity: a coefficient of 1.8 means a 1% increase in Glenwood Springs flow is associated with a 1.8% increase at Lees Ferry. This super-linear amplification makes physical sense — flow accumulates from tributaries between the two gauges, so an above-average headwater year compounds as it moves downstream.

Rankings do change after normalization — gauges with smaller drainage areas but high runoff intensity rise in relative rank, while large-drainage mainstem gauges fall. Per-area normalization removes the confounding effect of watershed size, enabling comparison of runoff intensity rather than total volume — a more meaningful metric when asking which sub-basin is proportionally wet or dry. Raw discharge is appropriate for Compact accounting, reservoir operations, and consumptive use calculations where total water volume is what matters. Normalized discharge is preferred when comparing rainfall-runoff response across sites, identifying anomalously high-contributing sub-basins, or diagnosing which tributary is disproportionately dry in a drought year.

This is not a pattern of isolated dry years — the persistent concentration of below-threshold periods through the mid-2010s and early 2020s represents a sustained baseline shift in which flows that were historically rare have become the new normal. For Compact management this means that years previously sufficient to meet delivery obligations are increasingly years of shortage, raising questions about the long-term sustainability of the 1922 allocation framework.

The record shows a clear structural shift beginning around water year 2000, with below-median years becoming dominant through the 2000s–2020s compared to the roughly balanced distribution of the 1980s and 1990s. Water year 2023 stands out as a dramatic exception — the exceptional atmospheric river winter produced above-median flow and represents the single wettest year in decades, partially reversing years of storage depletion in Lakes Powell and Mead. For Compact accounting, this sustained shift means that the 10-year average delivery calculation increasingly reflects drought conditions rather than the 20th-century hydrology on which the Compact’s allocations were based.




Question 6: Basin-Wide Trend Analysis

anomaly <- annual |>
  left_join(baseline_stats, by = c("site_no", "name")) |>
  mutate(anomaly = (total_flow - baseline_mean) / baseline_sd)

nrow(anomaly) == nrow(annual)

The post-2000 drought signal appears across all gauges simultaneously, indicating a basin-wide climatic forcing rather than localized conditions — no gauge is clearly isolated from the pattern. The most persistent negative signal accumulates at the lower mainstem gauges (Lees Ferry, Davis Dam), where drought effects compound from the entire upstream watershed. Two basin-wide anomaly years stand out clearly: 2002 (a severe drought year following a warm, dry winter connected to El Niño collapse) and 2023 (a strongly positive anomaly driven by a series of atmospheric rivers that delivered exceptional Rocky Mountain snowpack). Simultaneous basin-wide anomalies reveal something a single-gauge record cannot: they confirm that the signal is large-scale atmospheric forcing, not local watershed variability — which has direct implications for forecast skill and management planning horizons.

a.

annual_spatial <- annual |>
  left_join(select(site_meta, site_no, dec_lat_va, dec_long_va),
            by = "site_no")

nrow(annual_spatial) == nrow(annual)

[1] TRUE

center <- annual_spatial |>
  group_by(water_year) |>
  summarize(
    weighted_lon = sum(dec_long_va * total_flow, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_flow, na.rm = TRUE),
    weighted_lat = sum(dec_lat_va  * total_flow, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_flow, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Actual data range: lon ~-112° (stable), lat ~36.4–37.3°N
head(center)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  water_year weighted_lon weighted_lat

1       1980        -112.         36.6

b.

western_states <- map_data("state") |>
  filter(region %in% c("arizona", "nevada", "utah", "colorado",
                        "new mexico", "wyoming", "california"))

p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = western_states,
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray90", color = "white") +
  geom_path(data = center,
            aes(x = weighted_lon, y = weighted_lat, color = water_year),
            linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = center,
             aes(x = weighted_lon, y = weighted_lat, color = water_year),
             size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "steelblue", high = "firebrick", name = "Water Year") +
  coord_fixed(1.3, xlim = c(-116, -104), ylim = c(33, 42)) +
  labs(title    = "Flow-Weighted Spatial Center of Colorado Basin",
       subtitle = "Blue = earlier years, Red = recent years",
       x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p2 <- ggplot(center, aes(x = water_year, y = weighted_lat)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick",
              linetype = "dashed", se = TRUE) +
  labs(title   = "Weighted Mean Latitude Over Time",
       x = "Water Year", y = "Weighted Mean Latitude (°N)",
       caption = "Source: USGS NWIS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p1 | p2








c.

The two years with the most northward-shifted center are water year 1993 and water year 2023, both spiking above approximately 37°N. Both were driven by exceptional upper Rocky Mountain snowpack — 1993 by a strong El Niño that delivered prolonged winter storms to the headwaters, and 2023 by a series of atmospheric river events that produced record snowpack across Colorado and Utah. What they share physically is the same mechanism: disproportionately high snowmelt runoff at the northern headwater gauges (Roaring Fork, CO-UT border) temporarily inflated their contribution to total basin flow, pulling the weighted center north. These two years serve as natural experiments, isolating the signature of upper basin snowmelt dominance. The long-term upward trend in weighted latitude reflects the relative resilience of upper Rocky Mountain snowpack compared to the southern tributaries (San Juan, Colorado River near Grand Canyon), which have experienced more persistent flow declines under warming and reduced Arizona monsoon reliability. As the southern gauges contribute proportionally less over time, the center drifts north — a pattern that matters for downstream managers because it signals that the basin is increasingly dependent on a narrow northern snowmelt window rather than a distributed multi-season supply.







Note



Grading note: Students must identify 1993 and 2023 specifically. El Niño (1993) and atmospheric rivers (2023) are the correct physical causes. Award partial credit if students identify the spike years correctly but misattribute the cause. The long-term trend interpretation should mention either southern tributary decline or upper basin resilience — both are defensible.





Question 8: Seasonal Regimes and Peak Timing
a & b.

flow_seasonal <- flow_meta |>
  mutate(
    season = case_when(
      month %in% 4:6   ~ "Snowmelt",
      month %in% 7:9   ~ "Monsoon",
      month %in% 10:12 ~ "Low-flow",
      month %in% 1:3   ~ "Winter"
    ),
    season = factor(season, levels = c("Snowmelt", "Monsoon", "Low-flow", "Winter"))
  )

seasonal_summary <- flow_seasonal |>
  group_by(site_no, name, water_year, season) |>
  summarize(total_flow = sum(Flow,          na.rm = TRUE),
            norm_flow  = sum(flow_per_sqmi, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups    = "drop")

c.

peak_timing <- flow_meta |>
  group_by(site_no, name, water_year) |>
  slice_max(roll7, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(peak_doy = yday(Date))

peak_timing |>
  filter(site_no == "09380000") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = water_year, y = peak_doy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick", se = TRUE) +
  labs(title    = "Day of Peak 7-Day Flow at Lees Ferry by Water Year",
       subtitle = "A declining trend indicates earlier peak timing",
       x = "Water Year", y = "Day of Year of Peak Flow",
       caption = "Source: USGS NWIS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








d.

The peak timing trend at Lees Ferry shows a modest but detectable decline over the 44-year record — peak runoff is arriving roughly 1–2 weeks earlier compared to 1980, consistent with earlier snowmelt onset documented across the western US. The trend is visible in the regression line but has wide scatter, reflecting year-to-year variability in storm timing and snowpack depth that can shift the peak by weeks in either direction. Operationally, earlier peak timing compresses the window for reservoir filling: if peak runoff arrives in late April rather than mid-May, water managers must be ready to capture that pulse earlier — while still managing flood risk — and face reduced flexibility for timing summer storage. It also shortens the late-season baseflow period that sustains instream flows for fish and downstream agricultural deliveries.




Question 9: Predicting Lees Ferry from Upstream Conditions
a.

lees_model_data <- annual |>
  filter(site_no == "09380000") |>
  select(water_year, lees_flow = total_flow) |>
  left_join(
    annual |>
      filter(site_no == "09085000") |>
      select(water_year, glenwood_flow = total_flow),
    by = "water_year"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    seasonal_summary |>
      filter(site_no == "09380000") |>
      group_by(water_year) |>
      slice_max(total_flow, n = 1) |>
      select(water_year, season),
    by = "water_year"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(glenwood_flow), !is.na(lees_flow)) |>
  mutate(log_lees     = log(lees_flow),
         log_glenwood = log(glenwood_flow))

# Should be ~44 rows
nrow(lees_model_data)

[1] 45


b.

mod <- lm(log_lees ~ log_glenwood * season, data = lees_model_data)

  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared, p.value, AIC) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 4))) |>

The model achieves R² = 0.855 (adjusted R² = 0.828), explaining 85% of variance in log-annual discharge at Lees Ferry — the overall model is highly significant (p = 1.1 × 10⁻¹³). The log_glenwood coefficient of approximately 1.80 is an elasticity greater than 1, meaning a 1% increase in Roaring Fork flow is associated with a ~1.8% increase at Lees Ferry; this super-linear amplification is physically expected because flow accumulates from intermediate tributaries between the two gauges, so an above-average headwater year compounds as it moves downstream. The significant negative interaction terms for Monsoon, Low-flow, and Winter seasons indicate that the upstream-downstream coupling is strongest during Snowmelt and considerably weaker at other times — during the Monsoon season, for example, much of the precipitation falls on the lower basin in spatially isolated convective events that Roaring Fork cannot predict, and reservoir operations between the two gauges further buffer the relationship in the shoulder seasons.




Question 10: Model Evaluation
a.

aug <- augment(mod, data = lees_model_data)

b.

ggplot(aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = log_lees, color = season)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm",
              color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Season") +
  labs(title    = "Predicted vs. Actual Log Annual Discharge at Lees Ferry",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect prediction (1:1)",
       x = "Predicted log(cfs-days)", y = "Actual log(cfs-days)",
       caption = "Source: USGS NWIS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








c.

ggplot(aug, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title   = "Distribution of Model Residuals",
       x = "Residual", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








d.

The visible outlier in the scatter plot is water year 2023, which sits clearly above the 1:1 line — actual flow substantially exceeded the model’s prediction. This is expected: the model was trained on 1980–2022 conditions, and 2023’s exceptional atmospheric river snowpack was well outside the historical training envelope; the model cannot extrapolate to years it has never seen. Residuals are approximately normally distributed and centered near zero, with a slightly heavier right tail driven primarily by the 2023 outlier — the linear model in log space is appropriate for this data. Two predictors that would most improve the model are: (1) peak spring SWE from SNOTEL stations in the upper basin, which would directly capture snowpack magnitude and can be accessed via dataRetrieval months before melt — adding this could capture the 2023 anomaly by reflecting the exceptional snowpack signal; and (2) Lake Powell storage change, which buffers or amplifies the Glenwood–Lees Ferry relationship depending on whether the Bureau of Reclamation is filling or releasing, and whose exclusion likely explains much of the residual scatter in drought years when reservoir operations dominate the signal.







Note



Grading note: Water year 2023 must be identified as the outlier for full credit. Accept any explanation that references exceptional snowpack or out-of-sample conditions. For part (d), any two physically defensible predictors with clear mechanistic justification earn full credit. SWE and reservoir operations are the strongest answers but are not the only correct ones.

Quarto is the evolution of R Markdown — same authoring paradigm, modernized syntax and expanded scope:

How filter() Works: Boolean Vectors
Under the hood, filter() creates a boolean vector (all TRUE or FALSE) and keeps only the rows where the condition is TRUE.


Base R subsetting:

# Create a boolean vector
lifeExp_condition <- gapminder$lifeExp < 40
table(lifeExp_condition)
#> lifeExp_condition
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  1580   124

# This is what filter() does internally
head(gapminder[lifeExp_condition, ])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
#> # ℹ 3 more rows


Using filter():

# Much cleaner syntax
filter(gapminder, lifeExp < 40)
#> # A tibble: 124 × 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333      779.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
#> # ℹ 121 more rows








Note


filter() is cleaner and more readable, but it’s doing exactly what base R subsetting does: keeping rows where the condition is TRUE, dropping rows where it’s FALSE or NA.

select() — Base R Equivalence
Under the hood, select() is doing column subsetting — the same operation as base R.


Base R column subsetting:

# Bracket notation [rows, cols]
gapminder[, c("country", "lifeExp")]

# Extract single column
gapminder[["lifeExp"]]

# Dollar sign shorthand
gapminder$lifeExp


Using select():

# Much cleaner syntax
gapminder |>
  select(country, lifeExp)
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 2
#>   country     lifeExp
#>   <fct>         <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan    28.8
#> 2 Afghanistan    30.3
#> 3 Afghanistan    32.0
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows








Note


select() is syntactic layer on top of base R’s column subsetting. It’s more readable and composable with pipes.

title: Week 1 | Day 2
text:
mutate() — Base R Equivalence
Under the hood, mutate() is column assignment — the same operation as base R.

# Base R column assignment
gapminder$gdp <- gapminder$pop * gapminder$gdpPercap

# Remove a column (assign to NULL)
gapminder$gdpPercap <- NULL


Using mutate():

gapminder |>
  mutate(gdp = pop * gdpPercap,
         gdpPercap = NULL) 
#> # A tibble: 1,704 × 6
#>   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop         gdp
#>   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>       <dbl>
#> 1 Afghanistan Asia       1952    28.8  8425333 6567086330.
#> 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934 7585448670.
#> 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083 8758855797.
#> # ℹ 1,701 more rows









Note


mutate() builds on base R assignment but allows you to chain operations with the pipe and reference newly created columns within the same call.

Now Let’s Apply Them
We’ll cover the core concepts of SQL indirectly:

filter() = WHERE
select() = SELECT
mutate() = computed columns
summarize() + group_by() = GROUP BY + aggregate functions
arrange() = ORDER BY

The grammar transfers directly. SQL is the language of databases; dplyr is the language of R data frames. They solve the same class of problems.

Now let’s walk through each verb with concrete examples. You’ll see how they work in isolation, then how they compose into powerful pipelines.

text:
Why Vector Tiles?
Raster tiles (PNG/JPEG basemaps) are pre-computed images — styling is baked in.
Vector tiles are GeoJSON delivered at tile level — styling happens client-side, so:

One dataset, infinite styling options (day/night, language, theme)
File sizes 10–100× smaller than raster tiles
Client applies filters, clustering, legends on the fly
Standard format: .mbtiles or .pmtiles

Use case: You have 500k city points. Instead of pre-rendering a billion zoom-specific PNGs, ship vector tiles (20MB) + style JSON (5KB) and let the user’s browser render on demand.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: The Pipeline: GeoJSON → Tiles → PMTiles → Styled Map
text:
The Pipeline: GeoJSON → Tiles → PMTiles → Styled Map
Step 1: Prepare GeoJSON

cities <- us_cities |> 
  st_transform(4326) |>      # ALWAYS 4326 for web
  select(name, population, state)

st_write(cities, "cities.geojson")

Step 2: Build Vector Tiles with tippecanoe (command line, not R)
# Create .mbtiles from GeoJSON
# -Z0 -z14: zoom levels 0 (world) to 14 (neighborhood)
# --coalesce-fraction 0.8: merge nearby points to reduce file size
tippecanoe -o cities.mbtiles -Z0 -z14 \
  --coalesce-fraction 0.8 \
  cities.geojson
Step 3: Convert to .pmtiles (Optional, Recommended)
.mbtiles is SQLite-based; .pmtiles is a single portable file optimized for HTTP range requests:
# Option A: Use official pmtiles tool
pmtiles convert cities.mbtiles cities.pmtiles

# Option B: Python tool
pip install pmtiles
pmtiles convert cities.mbtiles cities.pmtiles
Step 4: Style with freestiler (R)
freestiler generates Mapbox/MapLibre JSON styles programmatically:

library(freestiler)

# Start with defaults
style <- freestile()

# Set background
style <- style |> add_background(color = "#f0f0f0")

# Add circle layer for points
style <- style |> 
  add_vector_layer(
    id = "cities",
    source = "cities",       # must match tiles source name
    type = "circle",
    paint = list(
      "circle-radius" = list("base" = 5, "stops" = list(c(5, 4), c(15, 12))),
      "circle-color" = list("base" = "#1f77b4"),
      "circle-stroke-color" = "#ffffff",
      "circle-stroke-width" = 1,
      "circle-opacity" = 0.8
    )
  )

# Add text labels at higher zoom
style <- style |> 
  add_vector_layer(
    id = "cities-labels",
    source = "cities",
    type = "symbol",
    layout = list(
      "text-field" = "{name}",
      "text-size" = 11,
      "text-offset" = list(0, 1.5)
    ),
    paint = list(
      "text-color" = "#000000",
      "text-halo-color" = "#ffffff",
      "text-halo-width" = 1
    ),
    minzoom = 6   # labels only above zoom 6
  )

# Write to JSON for the browser
jsonlite::write_json(style, "style.json", pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)

Step 5: Serve with MapLibre GL JS (in HTML/JavaScript)
<link href="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@3/dist/maplibre-gl.css" rel="stylesheet" />
<script src="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@3/dist/maplibre-gl.js"></script>

<div id="map" style="width: 100%; height: 600px;"></div>

<script>
  const map = new maplibregl.Map({
    container: 'map',
    style: './style.json',  // your freestiler output
    center: [-95, 40],      // continental US center
    zoom: 3
  });
  
  // Add pmtiles source
  map.on('load', () => {
    map.addSource('cities', {
      type: 'vector',
      url: 'pmtiles:///path/to/cities.pmtiles'
    });
  });
</script>
Or use MapLibre with @pmtiles/protomaps-leaflet in Leaflet:
#| eval: false
# R + leaflet approach (hybrid)
# Leaflet with PMTiles can integrate vector tiles + Leaflet interactivity

library(leaflet)
# (Note: pmtiles support in R is emerging; JavaScript/HTML is currently easier)

section: 4. The CRS Constraint: Web Maps Are Always 4326
text:
4. The CRS Constraint: Web Maps Are Always 4326
You learned EPSG:5070 for analysis (equal-area, no distortion).
Web browsers have no choice: all maps use WGS84 (EPSG:4326).
Why? Web tiles are pre-rendered globally in a Mercator grid. Only works in 4326.
The workflow:

## 1. Analyze in EPSG:5070 (accurate areas, distances)
watersheds <- st_read("shp") |> st_transform(5070) |> 
  mutate(area_km2 = drop_units(st_area(.) / 1e6))

## 2. Transform to 4326 ONLY when publishing to web
watersheds_web <- watersheds |> st_transform(4326)

## 3. Map it
leaflet(watersheds_web) |> addPolygons(color = ~color_by_area(area_km2))

This is the ONLY time you transform away from your analysis CRS.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: 5. Map Tiles: A Tiled Web Map (Slippy Map)
text:
5. Map Tiles: A Tiled Web Map (Slippy Map)
A tiled web map seamlessly joins dozens of 256×256 pixel images streamed over the internet.
Google Maps conventions (adopted industry-wide):

Each tile is exactly 256 pixels × 256 pixels
At zoom level 0, the entire world fits in one 256px tile
Each zoom level doubles in both X and Y → replaces 1 tile with 4
About 22 zoom levels are sufficient for Earth to building-level detail
Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857) is standard — includes latitude limits at approximately ±85°

OpenStreetMap “Slippy Map” standard:

URL format: http://.../{Z}/{X}/{Y}.png

Z = zoom level (0–22)
X = column index (0 at left, increases rightward)
Y = row index (0 at top, increases downward)

All tiles are PNG images
Worldwide coverage at all zoom levels

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
6. Zoom Levels & Tile Coordinates
At zoom 0, the entire Earth is one 256×256 pixel tile. As you zoom in, tiles split exponentially:

Zoom 0: 1 tile (1×1 grid)
Zoom 1: 4 tiles (2×2 grid)
Zoom Z: \(4^Z\) tiles total

At zoom 18 (street-level), there are ~68 billion tiles covering Earth.
Tile coordinates & URLs:
Tiles are indexed by (Z, X, Y) with (0,0) at top-left:
https://tile-server.org/{Z}/{X}/{Y}.png
Example: UCSB at zoom 18
https://a.tile.openstreetmap.org/18/43803/104352.png

Tile column 43803, row 104352 → PNG of UCSB streets
Each pixel ≈ 1.2 meters on the ground

Key insight: Each zoom increments X/Y quadrants, so user pans/zooms seamlessly fetch neighboring tiles client-side.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
7. Tile Size & Resolution Math
The horizontal distance covered by each tile depends on latitude and zoom level:
\[S_{tile} = C \cdot \cos(latitude) / 2^{zoomlevel}\]
where \(C = 2\pi \cdot 6,378,137\) m (Earth’s equatorial circumference).
One pixel in that tile represents:
\[S_{pixel} = S_{tile} / 256\]
Example: UCSB (lat = 34.414°, zoom = 18)

C <- 2 * pi * 6378137.00
S_tile <- C * cos(34.4140 * pi / 180) / 2^18
S_pixel <- S_tile / 256

cat("Tile covers:", round(S_tile), "meters\n")
cat("Each pixel:", round(S_pixel, 2), "meters\n")

At zoom 18, each pixel is roughly 1.2 meters on the ground — street-level detail.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
text:
8. Web Mercator Projection & Distortion
All web tiles use Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), a cylinder projection that:

Preserves shapes locally (locally conformal) — good for navigation
Severely distorts high latitudes — Greenland looks huge, Antarctica is cut off
Latitude limits at ±85° — mathematically, Mercator is undefined at ±90°

Why the distortion?
Mercator inflates distances north-south exponentially with latitude:
\[y = \ln(\tan(\pi/4 + \text{lat}/2))\]

Equator: 256 pixels ≈ 40,000 km (accurate)
60° latitude: same 256 pixels ≈ 20,000 km (stretched 2×)
Greenland (70°): drags to continent size despite being 1/14th of Africa







Important


Web Mercator distorts areas, angles, and distances. Never use it for analysis. Use EPSG:5070 (equal-area), UTM (equidistant), or other appropriate CRS for all calculations. Transform to 4326 only at publication.

title: Week 2 | Day 2
section: 9. User Zooming: The Pyramid in Action
text:
9. User Zooming: The Pyramid in Action
When a user zooms in:

Browser requests 4 new tiles to replace the 1 parent tile
New tiles are at zoom level Z+1 with finer detail
Process repeats smoothly — pan, pinch, scroll wheel

When a user zooms out:

Browser requests 1 coarser parent tile (zoom level Z-1)
Old 4 tiles are discarded
Map simplifies smoothly

Result: Users experience seamless, fast panning/zooming because: - Only visible tiles download - Pre-rendered tiles are cached on CDNs - Browser memory is minimal (a few MB of tiles at a time)

Clustering benefits:

Reduces clutter — 5k points become 5–10 clusters initially

✅ Users browse hierarchically (zoom-in behavior)
❌ 100k+ points (too slow even with clustering; use WebGL or vector tiles)
❌ Real-time streaming (server-side clustering is static)

24. Vector Tiles & Styling with freestiler
Why vector tiles: client requests small tiles of vector data and applies style client-side — massive datasets become browsable.
Pipeline overview:

Prepare GeoJSON or NDJSON.
Create .mbtiles using tippecanoe (OS-level tool).
Optionally convert .mbtiles → .pmtiles for a single portable file.
Author style JSON using freestiler (R) to produce Mapbox/MapLibre style JSON.
Serve .pmtiles via static hosting or pmtiles-aware server and point MapLibre/Mapbox/leaflet-mapbox-gl.js at the tile endpoint.

Commands (guide only):

# convert to pmtiles (requires pmtiles CLI or Python tool)

freestiler (R) example: produce a Mapbox-style JSON from R objects

library(freestiler)
# create a basic style and write to file
style <- freestiler::freestile() |> 
  add_background("#fff") |> 
  add_vector_layer(source = "cities", paint = list("circle-color" = "#1f78b4"))
writeLines(jsonlite::toJSON(style, auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE), "style.json")

Client side: MapLibre or mapbox-gl in the browser reads style.json and tiles endpoint.
Notes: mapdeck uses deck.gl; for production without Mapbox, serve styles via MapLibre + pmtiles host.

24. Vector Tiles & PMTiles
Vector tiles: GeoJSON delivered at tile level—styling happens client-side (1M+ features, 10–100× smaller files than raster).
Quick pipeline:
# 1. Create tiles from GeoJSON
tippecanoe -o data.mbtiles -Z0 -z14 data.geojson

# 2. Convert to PMTiles (single portable file)
pmtiles convert data.mbtiles data.pmtiles

# 3. Serve via static host or Python
python -m http.server 8000
In R with freestiler (style authoring):

library(freestiler)

style <- freestile() |>
  add_background("#fff") |>
  add_vector_layer(
    source = "cities",
    type = "circle",
    paint = list("circle-color" = "#1f77b4", "circle-radius" = 5)
  )

jsonlite::write_json(style, "style.json", auto_unbox = TRUE)

Why PMTiles? Single file, HTTP range requests, portable—host on GitHub Pages or static CDN.

text:
Why CRS Matters for Water Resources
Before we start: the single most common silent error in spatial water resources analysis.


USGS NWIS gauge coordinates → WGS84 (EPSG:4326)
NHDPlus HR flowlines → NAD83 (EPSG:4269)

3DEP elevation → varies by tile



These are different coordinate systems. The differences are small (~1–3 meters for NAD83 vs. WGS84) but:

Joining gauges to their catchments? Wrong
Snapping gauges to the nearest flowline? Wrong
Computing distance from a gauge to a dam? Wrong









Important


Always check CRS before any spatial join or distance calculation. We’ll learn the three tools that make this automatic.

title: Week 2
section: Why Classes Matter: One Data Structure, Many Behaviors
text:
Why Classes Matter: One Data Structure, Many Behaviors
You’ve already used S3 classes in tidyverse without noticing. The same object type can behave differently based on its class.
Understanding S3 classes in R explains:

Why print() on a tibble looks different than a regular data.frame



Why filter() on grouped data filters within each group instead of globally




Why summarize() on a grouped_df produces a different output shape



This is the callback pattern — R looks at an object’s class and dispatches to the right function. Later, sf will extend data.frame with spatial methods that work the same way.

title: Week 2
text:
Adding Class: Matrix → Data Frame
A class is metadata attached to an object telling R how to interpret and operate on it:

# Start with a matrix — just numbers in rows and columns
v <- c(1,2,3,4,5,6)
class(v)
#> [1] "numeric"
m <- matrix(v, nrow = 3)
class(m)
#> [1] "matrix" "array"
m
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    4
#> [2,]    2    5
#> [3,]    3    6


# Add class metadata: "this is a data frame"
df <- as.data.frame(m)
class(df)
#> [1] "data.frame"
df
#>   V1 V2
#> 1  1  4
#> 2  2  5
#> 3  3  6

Same data. But now df has column names, printed summary, and methods that respect rectangular structure. The class changed the behavior without changing the underlying values.

title: Week 2
text:
Class Hierarchies: Adding Layers
Objects can have multiple classes in a hierarchy. Adding structure adds more classes:

# Plain data.frame
df <- data.frame(gauge = c("A", "B", "C"), flow = c(100, 120, 95))
class(df)
#> [1] "data.frame"

# Add grouping — now it has *two* classes
gdf <- group_by(df, gauge)
class(gdf)
#> [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

# Methods are dispatched: dplyr functions check for "grouped_df" first
slice(gdf, 1)  # respects grouping — one row per group, not one global row
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#> # Groups:   gauge [3]
#>   gauge  flow
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 A       100
#> 2 B       120
#> 3 C        95
slice(df, 1)   # no grouping — just one row total
#>   gauge flow
#> 1     A  100


The key insight: the same function behaves differently based on class. This is the callback mechanism. When you call slice(), R internally asks: “What class is this object?” and dispatches to the right implementation.

title: Week 2
section: Methods: Functions That Know Their Object’s Class
text:
Methods: Functions That Know Their Object’s Class
Every function that respects class has methods or versions specialized for each class:

# Base R example: print() has different methods
print.data.frame()   # specialized for data.frames
print.default()      # fallback for other objects

# You can list all methods for a class:
methods(class = "data.frame")   # all functions with .data.frame versions


select(), filter(), mutate() are dplyr verbs that have methods:

methods("filter")    # shows filter.data.frame, filter.grouped_df, filter.ts, etc.
#> [1] filter.data.frame* filter.sf*         filter.ts*        
#> see '?methods' for accessing help and source code

text:
The Dependencies Under sf
sf is powerful because it’s not built from scratch — it wraps three long standing C/C++ libraries, each with a focused job:

title: Week 2
text:
The Spatial Stack
Your R code:
sf::st_read("data.shp")      # I/O
sf::st_distance(a, b)        # Geometry
sf::st_transform(x, 4269)    # CRS








📦 GDAL


File I/O

Format translators
Reads/writes Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, GeoTIFF
Returns WKB geometry











🧭 PROJ


Coordinate Systems

Transforms between 10,000+ CRS definitions
Handles datum shifts & projections
Underlies st_transform()











⚙️ GEOS


Geometry Ops

Intersection, union, buffer, centroid
Distance calculations
Spatial predicates (st_intersects())

title: Week 2
text:
Why This Matters
Each library solves a hard problem:








Library
Solves
Water Resources Example




GDAL
“How do I read a shapefile or GeoPackage?”
Read NHD flowlines, USGS boundaries, stream gauges


PROJ
“How do I convert WGS84 to Albers?”
Transform NWIS gauges from GPS coordinates to federal projection


GEOS
“Is this point inside this polygon? What’s the distance?”
Snap gauge to nearest flowline, clip to basin



If we had to write these from scratch in R, it would take years. Instead, spatial computing in R benefits from decades of work by the OSGeo community.

title: Week 2
text:
The sf Wrapper

sf::sf_extSoftVersion()
#>           GEOS           GDAL         proj.4 GDAL_with_GEOS     USE_PROJ_H 
#>       "3.14.1"       "3.12.2"        "9.7.1"         "true"         "true" 
#>           PROJ 
#>        "9.7.1"

sf doesn’t reinvent these wheels. It:

Calls GDAL for I/O (st_read(), st_write())
Calls PROJ for CRS transformations (st_transform())
Calls GEOS for geometry operations (st_distance(), st_buffer(), spatial predicates)
Wraps results with S3 classes and methods so dplyr verbs (filter(), mutate(), select()) just work — same as tidyverse

This diagram shows the relationship: sf methods dispatch to GEOS for the heavy lifting, then return R objects.






Note


When you install the sf package on your machine, the R package manager compiles and links against GDAL, PROJ, and GEOS. If installation fails, it’s usually because one of these C/C++ libraries is missing from your system. This is why setting up spatial computing can be more complex than installing a pure-R package.

title: Week 2
text:
What Is a Simple Feature?

Simple features (ISO 19125-1:2004) is a standard describing how real-world objects can be represented in computers, with emphasis on their spatial geometry
It defines:

A class hierarchy of geometry types
A set of operations on those geometries
Binary and text encodings for storage and transfer




Widely implemented: PostGIS, ESRI ArcGIS, GDAL, GeoJSON — and sf in R
A subset of simple features (the big 7) forms the GeoJSON specification

title: Week 2
text:
What Is a Feature?
A feature is a thing in the real world — a river, a gauge, a watershed, a county.

Features often consist of other features:

A river system → a river → an outlet point
A watershed → sub-basins → individual reaches



The standard says: “A simple feature has both spatial and non-spatial attributes. Spatial attributes are geometry valued.”

The geometry describes where the feature is and how it is represented
A river’s geometry could be its watershed polygon, its mainstem linestring, or its outlet point — depending on the question

title: Week 2
text:
The Big 7 Geometry Types








Single
Description




POINT
Zero-dimensional — a single coordinate pair


LINESTRING
Sequence of points connected by straight line pieces — 1D


POLYGON
Closed ring with positive area — 2D; may have interior holes






Multi (same type)
Description




MULTIPOINT
Set of points


MULTILINESTRING
Set of linestrings


MULTIPOLYGON
Set of polygons






Mixed
Description




GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
Set of geometries of any type










Note


These 7 types cover virtually everything in water resources work: gauge locations (POINT), stream reaches (LINESTRING), watershed boundaries (POLYGON), and their multi-feature equivalents.

title: Week 2
text:
Dimensions
All geometries are composed of points defined in 2-, 3-, or 4-D space:

XY — standard 2D coordinates (longitude, latitude or easting, northing)
XYZ — adds altitude (elevation of stream bed, DEM surface)
XYM — adds a measure attribute independent of the feature (e.g., streamflow at a vertex — rarely used)
XYZM — both Z and M


Note: “dimension” here means coordinate dimension (XY vs XYZ), not whether the geometry has length or area:

m1 <- rbind(c(8,1), c(2,5), c(3,2))
st_dimension(st_multipoint(m1))    # 0 — point set, no length
#> [1] 0
st_dimension(st_linestring(m1))    # 1 — has length, no area
#> [1] 1

title: Week 2
text:
Valid Geometries
Rules for valid geometries:

LINESTRING — no self-intersections
POLYGON — rings must be closed
POLYGON — holes inside exterior only
POLYGON — rings touch at points only
POLYGON — no repeated paths







Warning


Run st_is_valid() to check your data. Fix invalid geometries with st_make_valid().

title: Week 2
text:
Empty Geometries
EMPTY geometries serve as “NA” placeholders for geometry types — they arise naturally from spatial operations:

(e <- st_intersection(st_point(c(0,0)), st_point(c(1,1))))
#> GEOMETRYCOLLECTION EMPTY
st_is_empty(e)
#> [1] TRUE

plot(st_point(c(0,0)), pch = 16)
plot(st_point(c(1,1)), add = TRUE, col = 'red', pch = 16)

title: Week 2
text:
Well-Known Text and Well-Known Binary
The simple feature standard defines two encodings:
Well-Known Text (WKT) — human-readable:

x <- st_linestring(matrix(10:1, 5))
st_as_text(x)
#> [1] "LINESTRING (10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)"

LINESTRING = type · parentheses contain points · points separated by commas · coordinates separated by spaces

Well-Known Binary (WKB) — machine-readable, fast, lossless:

st_as_binary(x)
#>  [1] 01 02 00 00 00 05 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 24 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 14 40
#> [26] 00 00 00 00 00 00 22 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 10 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 20 40 00
#> [51] 00 00 00 00 00 08 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 1c 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 40 00 00
#> [76] 00 00 00 00 18 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f

WKB is used to communicate with external libraries (GDAL, GEOS) and spatial databases. Converting back to R:

st_as_sfc("LINESTRING(10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)")[[1]]
#> LINESTRING (10 5, 9 4, 8 3, 7 2, 6 1)

title: Week 2
text:
Three Classes, One Object


🟢 sf — a data.frame with feature attributes and a geometry column (class: sf)
🔴 sfc — the geometry list-column (set of geometries)
🔵 sfg — individual simple feature geometry (one geometry per feature)








Important


This is the S3 class hierarchy in action. sf is a subclass of data.frame adding the geometry column and specialized methods. When you call filter() on an sf object, R looks at its class and dispatches to the spatial-aware filter.sf() method, which respects the geometry column. Same pattern as grouped_df from tidyverse.

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Simple Feature Geometry
sfg objects carry the geometry for a single feature. Storage rules:

A single POINT → numeric vector
Points in a LINESTRING or POLYGON ring → matrix (each row = a point)
Any other set → list


Creator functions (rarely used in practice — you usually read existing data):

(x <- st_point(c(1, 2)))
str(x)
#>  'XY' num [1:2] 1 2

(x <- st_linestring(matrix(c(1,2,3,4), ncol = 2)))
str(x)
#>  'XY' num [1:2, 1:2] 1 2 3 4

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Class Structure
All geometry objects have an S3 class indicating (1) dimension, (2) type, (3) superclass:

(pt  <- st_point(c(0, 1)))
attributes(pt)
#> $class
#> [1] "XY"    "POINT" "sfg"

(pt2 <- st_point(c(0, 1, 4)))   # XYZ
attributes(pt2)
#> $class
#> [1] "XYZ"   "POINT" "sfg"

title: Week 2
text:
sfg: Same Points, Different Meaning
The same coordinate matrix creates geometries with entirely different dimensionality:

m1 <- rbind(c(8,1), c(2,5), c(3,2))

(mp <- st_multipoint(m1))   # zero-dimensional point set
(ls <- st_linestring(m1))   # one-dimensional line

st_dimension(mp); st_length(mp)
#> [1] 0
#> [1] 0
st_dimension(ls); st_length(ls)
#> [1] 1
#> [1] 10.37338

title: Week 2
text:
Mixed Geometries and GEOMETRYCOLLECTION
Sets of features can have heterogeneous geometry types — type becomes GEOMETRY:



(g <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0,0)),
             st_linestring(rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1)))))
#> Geometry set for 2 features 
#> Geometry type: GEOMETRY
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA


Filter by type with st_is:

g |> st_is("LINESTRING")
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE

st_sf(geometry = g) |>
  filter(st_is(geometry, "LINESTRING"))
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 0 fields
#> Geometry type: LINESTRING
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA
#>                geometry
#> 1 LINESTRING (0 0, 1 1)



When intersections produce mixed types, use GEOMETRYCOLLECTION and extract:

pt   <- st_point(c(1,0))
ls   <- st_linestring(matrix(c(4,3,0,0), ncol=2))
poly <- st_polygon(list(matrix(c(5.5,7,7,6,5.5,0,0,-0.5,-0.5,0), ncol=2)))
j    <- st_geometrycollection(list(pt, ls, poly))

st_collection_extract(j, "POLYGON")

title: Week 2
text:
Casting: Feature vs. Set Level
Casting operates at the feature level, not the set level:

rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(1,0), c(0,1)) |>
  st_linestring() |>
  st_cast("POINT")   # ⚠️ converts ONE line to ONE point — not what you want
#> Warning in st_cast.LINESTRING(st_linestring(rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 1), c(1, :
#> point from first coordinate only
#> POINT (0 0)


To extract individual points, work at the set level (sfc):

(p <- rbind(c(0,0), c(1,1), c(1,0), c(0,1)) |>
   st_linestring() |>
   st_sfc() |>           # create a SET of one geometry
   st_cast("POINT"))     # now produces 4 individual points
#> Geometry set for 4 features 
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 0 ymin: 0 xmax: 1 ymax: 1
#> CRS:           NA

sfc: Geometry List-Columns
st_sfc creates sets of geometries — what becomes the sticky list-column in sf objects:

(sfc <- st_sfc(st_point(c(0,1)), st_point(c(-3,2))))
#> Geometry set for 2 features 
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -3 ymin: 1 xmax: 0 ymax: 2
#> CRS:           NA
class(sfc)
#> [1] "sfc_POINT" "sfc"
attributes(sfc) |> names()
#> [1] "class"     "precision" "bbox"      "crs"       "n_empty"

The sfc object records for the whole set: precision, bounding box, CRS, and count of empty geometries.

title: Week 2
text:
Combine vs. Union
Combining geometries preserves interior boundaries. Unioning dissolves them.



(co_c <- st_combine(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84












(co_u <- st_union(co$geometry))
#> Geometry set for 1 feature 
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -109.0602 ymin: 36.99246 xmax: -102.0415 ymax: 41.00342
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

title: Week 2
text:
Combine + Cast: Borders as Lines

co_c_ml <- st_combine(co$geometry) |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")
co_u_ml <- st_union(co$geometry)   |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")









Tip


This distinction matters constantly in water resources: county boundaries vs. watershed boundaries, stream reaches vs. the river network, individual gauge catchments vs. the basin outline.

title: Week 2
text:
What Makes Spatial Data Spatial?

The geometry alone is meaningless without knowing where on Earth those coordinates refer to. That’s the job of the Coordinate Reference System.

title: Week 2
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
A Coordinate Reference System (CRS) defines how spatial features relate to the surface of the Earth.
Two broad types:

Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) — locations on the curved surface of the Earth, measured in angular units (degrees)
Projected Coordinate System (PCS) — locations on a flat surface, measured in linear units (meters, feet)

In sf, three tools:



Function
Does




st_crs()
Retrieve CRS from an sf or sfc object


st_set_crs()
Set or replace CRS (no coordinate transformation)


st_transform()
Transform coordinates from one CRS to another

title: Week 2
text:
Geographic Coordinate Systems
A GCS identifies locations on the curved surface of the Earth using angular measurements from the center:

Latitude — vertical angle (North/South from equator)
Longitude — horizontal angle (East/West from prime meridian)
North and East are positive; South and West are negative


A GCS is defined by three components:

Ellipsoid — the mathematical model of Earth’s shape (flattened sphere, not perfect)
Datum — how the ellipsoid is anchored to the real Earth (locally fitted or globally centered)
Prime meridian — the origin of longitude (Greenwich, 0°E/W)

Why this matters: two datasets may use the same coordinates but different datums. The difference is small (sub-meter) but compounds in spatial joins and distance calculations.

title: Week 2
text:
Common Datums in Water Resources
Three datums account for most US data:









Datum
Acronym
Used by
Typical error vs. NAD83




North American Datum 1983
NAD83
NHDPlus, most USGS vector data
Reference datum


World Geodetic System 1984
WGS84
GPS, NWIS gauges, web maps
<1 meter in CONUS


NAD27 (historic)
NAD27
Legacy sources only
Can be 100+ meters off









Note


NAD83 and WGS84 differ by less than 1 meter for most of CONUS. But they are not the same CRS. Mixing them without explicit transformation introduces sub-meter errors that compound in spatial joins. Always check with st_crs(a) == st_crs(b) before joining.

title: Week 2
text:
Projected Coordinate Systems
A Projected Coordinate System (PCS) transforms the curved Earth onto a 2D plane. Every transformation introduces distortion.

Three main projection families:












Planar — flat surface touches globe at a point (best for polar regions)
Cylindrical — cylinder wraps around globe (world maps, Mercator)
Conic — cone around globe (mid-latitude areas, CONUS)

title: Week 2
text:
Spatial Properties and Distortion
Each type of projection prioritizes one property at the cost of others:








Property
Preserved by
Used for




Area
Equal-area (Albers)
Accurate area calculations, choropleth maps


Distance
Equidistant
Distance from a fixed center point


Shape
Conformal (Mercator)
Navigation, preserving local angles


Direction
Azimuthal
Navigation from a pole

title: Week 2
text:
Projection Choice: Water Resources Defaults
For CONUS analysis, use these defaults:






Important



Computing area (choropleth maps, watershed statistics) → EPSG:5070 (Albers Equal Area). This is the standard federal projection for CONUS.
Measuring distance (gauge to outlet, confluences, dam spacing) → Keep data in geographic (WGS84, EPSG:4326) and use st_distance() with default S2 spherical geometry — it’s geodesic and correct.
Sub-state local analysis → Use a local UTM zone (e.g., NAD83 / UTM zone 13) if you need projected planar distance.
Visualization/mapping → Use whatever looks right for your region (Web Mercator for web, Albers for print).

title: Week 2
text:
EPSG Codes and PROJ Strings
sf stores CRS in two ways:

EPSG code — integer ID for a known CRS (e.g., 4326 = WGS84 geographic)
PROJ4 string — generic text description understood by the PROJ library

Common codes for water resources work:








EPSG
Name
Use




4326
WGS84 geographic
GPS coordinates, web maps, NWIS gauges


4269
NAD83 geographic
NHDPlus, most USGS vector data


5070
NAD83 / Conus Albers
Area calculations, CONUS-wide analysis


26913–26915
UTM NAD83 zones 13–15
Local/state-level distance calculations



Practical rule: Use EPSG:5070 for CONUS area calculations; use a local UTM (e.g., NAD83 / UTM zones) for sub-state analyses.

st_crs(conus)$datum
